title: The business case: purpose & content
blurb: Why every project needs a business case, what goes in one, and how it is used from concept to benefits.
question: A council board is asked to approve £2m for a new parking app. Before it agrees, it wants a document that compares the options, including doing nothing, and sets the expected benefits against the costs and risks. Which document is this, and what is its purpose?

teach.body: Every project uses money, people and time that could be spent elsewhere. The business case is the document that argues it is worth it. Formally, it provides the justification for undertaking a project, by evaluating the benefits, costs and risks of alternative options and giving the rationale for the preferred solution. In plain English: it answers 'why are we doing this, and why this way?'

teach.h: The four jobs of a business case
items: Justify the investment: show the benefits outweigh the costs and risks.
Support go / no-go decisions at each decision gate.
Stay valid throughout: reviewed and updated as things change.
Be the basis for benefits realisation: the benefits it promises are what gets tracked.

teach.h: What goes in a business case

root.label: Business case
root.sub: Why this project, why this way?

teach.caption: Group the contents into four questions: what is the need, what could we do, what is it worth, and what will it take?

teach.h: Typical content and what each part answers
head: Section
Answers the question
rows: Why change, and how does it fit strategy?
Which option, and why that one?
What improves, and what gets worse?
What will it cost, and who pays?
Does the return justify the cost?
How will we buy what we need?

teach.body: Harbourside Council wants to cut queues at pay machines. Its business case sets out the need (complaints, slow payments, ageing machines), then compares three options. Doing nothing costs little now but complaints grow and machines fail. Repairing the machines is cheaper but fixes little. A parking app costs more but cuts queues and cash handling. The case recommends the app and shows why.

teach.caption: 'Do nothing' is the yardstick: every other option must show it is better than leaving things as they are.

teach.h: A living document through the life cycle

steps.label: Concept
steps.sub: Outline business case: need, options, rough costs

steps.label: Definition
steps.sub: Refined with better estimates and plans

steps.label: Decision gates
steps.sub: Is the project still justified? Go or no-go

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: Reviewed when costs, risks or benefits change

teach.caption: If the case stops adding up during delivery, the right answer may be to stop the project.

teach.body: The business case explains WHY the project is worth doing and which option is best. It is not the detailed plan for HOW the work will be done: that is the project management plan. So expect benefits, costs, risks, options and appraisal in a business case, not task lists, test scripts, meeting minutes or a full risk register.

teach.text: Exam distractors describe other documents: 'schedules the daily activities' (that is the plan), 'assigns roles to the team' (plan or RAM), 'records every risk' (risk register), 'defines how to engage each stakeholder' (engagement plan). The business case JUSTIFIES the investment.

items: Purpose: justify the investment by weighing benefits against costs and risks of the options.
It supports go / no-go decisions at gates and must stay valid throughout.
Typical content: need, options (incl. do nothing), preferred option, benefits and dis-benefits, costs, timescales, risks, investment appraisal, success criteria, commercial.
It is the basis for benefits realisation after the project.

summary: You can now explain that a business case justifies a project by weighing the benefits, costs and risks of the options, and list its typical content. You can also describe how it stays live from concept through decision gates to benefits realisation.

A.q: What is the main purpose of a business case?
options: To justify the investment in the project
To describe how the work will be delivered
To record the approved deployment baseline
To set out who will carry out each task
A.why: A business case provides the justification for undertaking the project by weighing benefits against costs and risks.

whyNot.1: How the work will be delivered is set out in the project management plan.
whyNot.2: The deployment baseline is the agreed plan for measuring delivery, not the justification.
whyNot.3: Who does each task is shown in the plan or a responsibility assignment matrix.

A.q: A board member asks whether the project's financial return justifies its cost. Which section of the business case answers this?
options: The strategic context
The delivery timescales
The investment appraisal
The success criteria
A.why: The investment appraisal assesses whether the expected return justifies the cost of the investment.

whyNot.0: The strategic context explains the background and need, not the financial return.
whyNot.1: Timescales say when the project will deliver, not whether it pays back.
whyNot.3: Success criteria say how success will be judged, not whether the return beats the cost.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT typical content of a business case?
options: Options considered
Major risks
Costs and funding
Daily task lists
A.why: Detailed daily tasks belong in delivery planning, not in the justification for the project.

whyNot.0: Options, including doing nothing, are a core part of a business case.
whyNot.1: Major risks are included so the decision takes account of uncertainty.
whyNot.2: Costs and how they will be funded are central to justifying the investment.

B.q: Complete the statement: a business case provides the ______ for undertaking a project.
options: specification
justification
governance
schedule
B.why: The business case is the justification: it sets out why the project is worth doing.

whyNot.0: A specification describes what an output must be, not why to invest.
whyNot.2: Governance is the framework of authority and decision-making, not a document's purpose.
whyNot.3: The schedule shows when work happens and sits in the plan.

B.q: Why should a business case include a 'do nothing' option?
options: It gives a yardstick to compare the others with
It is the option the sponsor is required to reject
It removes the need for an investment appraisal
It shows that work can be stopped at any time
B.why: Doing nothing is the baseline: every other option must show it is better than leaving things as they are.

whyNot.1: Doing nothing is sometimes the best choice; it is not automatically rejected.
whyNot.2: The options still need appraising; doing nothing is compared, not a replacement for appraisal.
whyNot.3: Stopping a project is a gate decision; the do-nothing option is about comparison.

B.q: Which TWO of the following would you expect to find in a business case? 1. Benefits and dis-benefits 2. Detailed test scripts 3. Costs and funding 4. Team meeting minutes
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: Benefits (and dis-benefits) and costs (and funding) are core business case content.

whyNot.0: Test scripts are quality control documents, not justification.
whyNot.1: Neither test scripts nor meeting minutes belong in a business case.
whyNot.3: Meeting minutes are a record of discussion, not part of the justification.

C.q: Mid-way through deployment, a competitor launches a cheaper product and the expected benefits fall sharply. What does this mean for the business case?
options: It needs no action because it was approved at concept
It should be reviewed to check the project is still justified
It should be replaced by the project management plan
It can be ignored until the benefits review after closure
C.why: The business case must remain valid throughout; a big change in benefits means reviewing whether the project should continue.

whyNot.0: Approval at concept does not end its job: the case is reviewed as things change.
whyNot.2: The plan explains how to deliver, not whether it is still worth delivering.
whyNot.3: Waiting until after closure could waste money on a project that is no longer justified.

C.q: A draft business case sets out the benefits and costs of each option but says nothing about risk. Why is this a weakness?
options: Risks belong only in the communication plan
Decision-makers would lack the full picture
Risks are added only after the benefits review
It means the do-nothing option cannot be used
C.why: A business case weighs benefits against costs AND risks; leaving risk out makes the justification incomplete.

whyNot.0: Major risks are typical business case content; the communication plan is about information flows.
whyNot.2: The benefits review is after delivery; risks must inform the decision before investing.
whyNot.3: The do-nothing option can still be compared; the gap is the missing risk information.

C.q: Which statement about dis-benefits in a business case is correct?
options: They are costs that were left out of the budget
They are benefits that arrive after the project closes
They are threats that have not happened yet
They are outcomes some stakeholders see as negative
C.why: A dis-benefit is an outcome perceived as negative by one or more stakeholders; the business case should show them alongside benefits.

whyNot.0: Missing costs are an estimating problem, not a dis-benefit.
whyNot.1: Benefits that arrive late are still benefits.
whyNot.2: Uncertain future threats are risks, recorded and managed as risks.

reteach.title: Think of it like buying a car
reteach.question: Before you spend thousands on a car, how do you convince yourself (or your partner) that it is worth it?

blocks.body: You start with the need: the old car keeps breaking down. You list options: keep the old one (do nothing), buy second-hand, or buy new. For each you weigh what you gain (reliability, lower fuel bills), what it costs, and what could go wrong. You pick the best option and say why. That is a business case. If fuel prices or your job change, you would rethink it.

blocks.h: The car decision as a business case
blocks.caption: Need, options, benefits, costs, risks and a reasoned choice: the same building blocks as a project business case.

blocks.text: The business case is the 'should we, and which way?' document. The step-by-step 'how' (collecting the car, insurance, paperwork) is the plan, not the case.

explain.body: A business case justifies the project. It weighs the benefits against the costs and risks and gives the rationale for the preferred option, so decision-makers can say go or no-go.

test.q: At a decision gate, the governance board mainly uses the business case to decide what?
options: Whether the project should continue
Which team member does each task
How defects will be logged and fixed
Which version of a document is current
test.why: The business case supports go / no-go decisions: is the project still worth doing?

whyNot.1: Task allocation is part of planning and the responsibility matrix.
whyNot.2: Defect handling belongs to quality control.

explain.body: A good case compares real alternatives, always including 'do nothing' as the yardstick, and then explains why the preferred option wins. Presenting only one option weakens the justification.

steps.label: Alternatives
steps.sub: Other ways to meet the need

steps.label: Preferred
steps.sub: Best balance of value and risk

test.q: Which option is included in a business case to show what happens if no investment is made?
options: The fallback plan
The do-nothing option
The preferred option
The contingency reserve
test.why: The do-nothing option shows the consequences of making no investment and acts as the comparison point.

whyNot.0: A fallback plan is a risk response used if a risk occurs.
whyNot.2: The preferred option is the recommended investment, not the no-investment case.
whyNot.3: A contingency reserve is time or money set aside for risk.

explain.body: The business case holds the need, options, benefits, dis-benefits, costs, timescales, major risks, investment appraisal, success criteria and commercial considerations. The detailed 'how' (schedules, procedures, responsibilities) lives in the project management plan.

test.q: Which item belongs in the business case rather than the project management plan?
options: The detailed resource plan
The communication schedule
The preferred option rationale
The configuration procedures
test.why: Explaining why the preferred option was chosen is part of justifying the investment.

whyNot.0: Resource planning is how the work will be delivered: the plan.
whyNot.1: Communication timing is part of the plan and the communication plan.
whyNot.3: Configuration procedures describe how items are controlled: the plan.

explain.body: The outline case is written in concept, refined in definition and reviewed at every decision gate and whenever costs, benefits or risks change. After delivery, the benefits it promised are tracked and reviewed.

test.q: When should a business case normally be reviewed?
options: Only once, at the end of concept
Only when the project is over budget
Only after the benefits are realised
At decision gates and on major change
test.why: The business case must remain valid throughout, so it is reviewed at gates and whenever a significant change affects it.

whyNot.0: A one-off review would miss changes that make the project unviable.
whyNot.1: Cost is only one trigger; benefits and risks can change too.
whyNot.2: By then it is too late to stop an unjustified project.
